content: Weaning and extubating preterm infants from intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) due to respiratory failure can be challenging. This difficulty is largely attributed to the underdeveloped respiratory drive in preterm infants, which predisposes them to hypercarbia (elevated carbon dioxide levels) and apnoea (temporary cessation of breathing). These issues are particularly pronounced in very preterm infants. Administering methylxanthines, such as theophylline or caffeine, prior to extubation may enhance respiratory stimulation and improve the likelihood of successful weaning from IPPV. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of prophylactic methylxanthine treatment on the success of extubation and the reduction of intubation and IPPV use in preterm infants. Additionally, the review aimed to assess the potential side effects associated with this treatment. The search strategy employed by the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group was utilized, encompassing databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials, MEDLINE, CINAHL, and EMBASE, with searches conducted up to July 2010. The inclusion criteria were randomized or quasi-randomized trials comparing methylxanthine treatment (theophylline or caffeine) with placebo or no treatment in preterm or low birth weight infants undergoing planned extubation. Seven studies met the inclusion criteria. The results demonstrated that methylxanthine treatment significantly reduced the risk of extubation failure within one week. The summary relative risk (RR) was 0.48 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.32 to 0.71), and the summary risk difference (RD) was -0.27 (95% CI -0.39 to -0.15). The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one extubation failure was 4 (95% CI 3 to 7). However, there was notable heterogeneity in the risk difference meta-analysis, likely due to the wide variation in baseline extubation failure rates among control groups (ranging from 20% to 100%). The largest trial included in the review, the CAP trial, did not report extubation rates but provided valuable data on other outcomes. Infants in the caffeine group exhibited lower rates of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) requiring surgical ligation, cerebral palsy, and death or major disability at 18 to 21 months of age. Additionally, infants receiving caffeine achieved earlier discontinuation of oxygen therapy, positive pressure ventilation, and endotracheal intubation, as measured by postmenstrual age. The authors concluded that methylxanthine therapy increases the likelihood of successful extubation in preterm infants within the first week of life. Furthermore, methylxanthine treatment, particularly caffeine, is associated with improved neurodevelopmental outcomes. Future trials should stratify infants by gestational age, as it is a more accurate indicator of immaturity than birth weight. Given its wider therapeutic margin, caffeine is recommended as the preferred methylxanthine for evaluation in comparison to placebo.
